subject: ela
description: Students compare and contrast how two authors present the same events, person, or topic in two informational texts (for example, a memoir written by a person and a biography written about that same person, or two news articles, two accounts, or two reference entries about one event). They identify the events or facts the two texts share; notice where the texts agree and where they differ in the details they include, the order they choose, the emphasis they give, and the conclusions they draw; recognize how each author's point of view, purpose, and relationship to the events (firsthand participant versus outside observer) shapes the presentation; and explain what a reader learns from reading both that could not be learned from either text alone. Because this is a reading standard, every item embeds the full text of both passages or excerpts it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer. There is no math.
subSkills: Identify the shared event, person, or topic that two informational texts both present
Determine each author's relationship to the events (firsthand participant in a memoir or first-person account versus outside observer in a biography or report) and how that shapes what they can tell
Identify facts or events that both texts agree on
Identify where the two texts differ in the details they include, what they leave out, the order they use, or the emphasis they give
Compare the authors' purposes and points of view and explain how those differences lead to different presentations of the same events
Explain what reading both texts together adds that reading only one would not, and support each comparison or contrast with specific evidence from both embedded texts

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the shared event or topic
problemArchetypes.example: Read the memoir excerpt and the biography excerpt embedded in the item, then name what both accounts are about: 'What event do both passages describe?' Answer names the single event or topic (for example, the day the inventor first tested her flying machine) that appears in both texts despite their different forms.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify a shared fact across both accounts
problemArchetypes.example: Read both embedded texts, then choose a detail both authors report: 'Which fact about the event do both the memoir and the biography include?' Answer is a detail genuinely present in both texts, not one that appears in only one of them.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify a difference in detail, emphasis, or order
problemArchetypes.example: Read both embedded accounts, then state one way they differ: 'What does the memoir include about the morning that the biography leaves out?' Answer names a real difference in the details chosen, the emphasis given, or the order of events, supported by the text.

problemArchetypes.name: Connect point of view to presentation
problemArchetypes.example: Read the firsthand account and the outside report embedded in the item, then explain how the author's position shapes the telling: 'Why is the memoir able to describe how the moment felt while the biography focuses on the facts and dates?' Answer links the firsthand or outside relationship of each author to what their account emphasizes.

problemArchetypes.name: Compare the authors' purposes
problemArchetypes.example: Read both embedded texts, then identify how the authors' purposes differ: 'How is the memoir author's purpose different from the biographer's purpose, and how does that show up in each text?' Answer names a genuine difference in purpose and points to evidence of it in each account.

problemArchetypes.name: What reading both texts adds
problemArchetypes.example: Read both embedded accounts, then explain the value of having both: 'What does a reader understand about the event from reading both passages that neither passage gives alone?' Answer states a real combined insight, such as how the inner experience from the memoir and the outside facts from the biography together give a fuller picture.

Easy.description: Two very short informational texts about the same event or person (for example, a 70 to 110 word memoir or first-person account and a 70 to 110 word biography or report passage), both embedded in the item, that share an obvious event with the difference between them signaled plainly on the surface. The task is to identify: name the shared event, name which account is firsthand and which is an outside view, pick a fact both texts state, or pick a detail that appears in only one. The shared content and the basic difference are stated or strongly signaled, requiring little inference.
constraints: Two short stimuli about the same event or person (a first-person account of about 70 to 110 words plus a biography or report passage of about 70 to 110 words) included in the prompt
The shared event, person, or topic is concrete and clearly the subject of both texts
Identify-level task: name the shared event, label which author is firsthand and which is an outside observer, match a stated fact to both texts, or find a detail present in only one
Differences in detail or emphasis are clear on the surface; no multi-step inference needed

Medium.description: Two moderate-length informational texts on the same event or person (for example, a 130 to 200 word memoir or firsthand account and a 130 to 200 word biography or article), both embedded in the item, that share an event but differ in the details chosen, the emphasis, or the order. The task requires analysis: explain a genuine difference in how each author presents the event, connect an author's point of view or relationship to the events to what their account emphasizes, or state a similarity or difference and support it. The answer is grounded in both texts but is not stated word for word.
constraints: Two moderate stimuli on the same event or person (a firsthand account of about 130 to 200 words plus a biography or article of about 130 to 200 words) included in the prompt
Both texts present the same event, but differ in detail selection, emphasis, or sequence rather than disagreeing on basic facts
Analyze-level task: explain how an author's purpose or point of view shapes the presentation, or name a similarity or difference and support it from both texts
Some inference required; each author's relationship to the events is shown through what they include and how they tell it rather than stated outright

Hard.description: Two longer or more layered informational texts about the same event or person (for example, a 220 to 340 word memoir or firsthand account and a 220 to 340 word biography, profile, or report), both embedded in the item, whose presentations diverge in emphasis, interpretation, or the conclusions each author draws. The task requires evaluation and synthesis: judge which account a reader should trust for a stated purpose, explain how the difference in the authors' points of view leads to a different overall impression of the event, or build a comparison that weighs evidence from several parts of each text and explains what reading both together reveals. Requires sustained inference across both texts.
constraints: Two longer stimuli about the same event or person (a firsthand account of about 220 to 340 words plus a biography, profile, or report of about 220 to 340 words) included in the prompt
The two accounts diverge in emphasis, interpretation, or the conclusions the authors reach, not only in surface detail

Evaluate or synthesize task: judge which account better serves a stated purpose, explain how differing points of view produce a different impression of the event, or explain what reading both together adds
Requires inference that draws on evidence from several places in both embedded texts

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student reads only one of the two texts and treats that single account as if it described both authors' presentations
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that accurately describes one text but is not true of the other, ignoring that the question asks about both accounts

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes two accounts of the same event must contradict each other, and labels a real point of agreement as a difference
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks an answer that frames the two authors as disagreeing about a fact when both texts actually report it the same way

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats a detail found in only one account as if both authors included it
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a detail that appears in only the memoir or only the biography as a fact both texts share

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses which author is the firsthand participant and which is the outside observer, swapping the memoir and the biography
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Attributes the firsthand, feelings-and-experience presentation to the biography and the outside, facts-and-dates presentation to the memoir, reversing the two authors' relationships to the events

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student notices a difference between the texts but fails to connect it to the authors' differing purposes or points of view
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Names a difference in the wording or details without linking it to why a participant and an outside observer would present the same event differently

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student states a comparison that sounds reasonable but is supported by neither embedded text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a plausible-sounding similarity or difference that has no evidence in either passage

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks one account simply repeats the other and cannot explain what reading both together adds
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the second text adds nothing new, ignoring that the firsthand experience and the outside facts together give a fuller understanding of the event than either alone
